analysis.one_liner: Requires all-in advertised prices and bans hidden junk fees for tickets, hotels, and phone bills.
analysis.headline: Introduced with two Democratic sponsors on December 4, 2025 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has had no hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force companies to show the full price of a purchase — including all mandatory fees — in the first price you see and keep that price from changing at checkout. It targets resort and booking fees at hotels and short-term rentals, surprise fees in concert and sports ticketing, phone and internet bills, and airline charges for bags, seat selection, and cancellations. It would also ban early termination fees on phone, internet, and cable service and give the FTC, FCC, and state attorneys general power to enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy live-event tickets, book hotels or short-term rentals, pay for phone, internet, or cable service, or fly. They would see the true total price up front, be protected from fees that change or exceed what was advertised, get full refunds including fees when a ticket sale falls through, avoid early termination fees with prorated credits after canceling, and see a single clear total price on telecom bills with the end date of any promotional rate disclosed before it expires. State attorneys general could sue on residents' behalf.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ticket buyers, travelers, and telecom customers

how_it_helps.text: Requires any covered company to clearly display the total price — including all mandatory fees and government charges — in every advertisement and at the first price shown, and forbids the price from changing during checkout.
Bans companies from imposing or advertising fees that are excessive or deceptive, with the FTC and courts judging whether a fee is proportional to the actual cost of the service.

Targets the ticketing market directly: sellers must disclose how many tickets exist at least 72 hours before a sale or presale, refund the full price including fees when refunds are given, and give full refunds on 'speculative' sales where the seller didn't actually hold the ticket.
Covers hotels, motels, inns, and short-term rentals booked for under six months, so resort fees and cleaning fees would have to appear in the advertised total price.
Bans phone, internet, and cable providers from charging early termination fees and requires a prorated credit for unused days in the billing cycle after cancellation.
Requires telecom bills and ads to show one clear aggregate price, and forces providers to disclose when an introductory rate ends and what the post-promotion rate will be at least 60 days ahead.

Requires airlines to report quarterly to the Transportation Department on revenue from ancillary fees like checked bags, seat selection, and cancellation charges, with the results published in a public comparison across carriers.
Enforceable by the FTC as an unfair or deceptive practice, and by state attorneys general suing on behalf of their residents for injunctions and restitution.

analysis.who_pays: Ticketing companies and resale platforms, hotels and short-term rental booking platforms, phone/internet/cable providers, and airlines, which would lose fee revenue they now collect from consumers who don't see the full price until checkout. Some advertised base prices would rise as fees get folded into the sticker price, but the total a consumer pays should fall. The FTC, FCC, and Transportation Department would take on new rulemaking and enforcement work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ticketing, lodging, telecom, and airline companies

drawbacks.text: The ban on 'excessive' fees turns on whether a fee is 'reasonable and proportional' to the cost of the service — an open-ended standard that invites years of litigation and inconsistent outcomes decided by the FTC, FCC, or individual courts.
Compliance burdens fall on all covered businesses, including small hotels, inns, and short-term rental operators, and some of those costs could be passed through in prices.

The airline section only requires quarterly reporting and publication of ancillary fee revenue — it does not cap bag, seat-selection, or cancellation fees or otherwise stop airlines from charging them.
Most of the bill works through new FTC and FCC rulemakings, which take years to propose, finalize, and survive legal challenge, so relief for consumers would be slow even if it passed.
When the FTC sues a company, state attorneys general are barred from bringing a separate case against that same defendant while the federal action is pending, which could slow some state enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real and direct: the bill attacks the gap between the advertised price and the checkout price in ticketing, lodging, telecom, and air travel, and gives regulators and state attorneys general tools to police it. The main honest concerns are design, not intent — the 'excessive' standard is vague, the airline piece is transparency-only, and enforcement depends on slow agency rulemaking. On balance the costs fall on companies whose business models rely on fees that consumers can't see in advance, and the bill explicitly preserves companies' ability to charge for unreturned equipment or outstanding device costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it — no hearing, no vote, no floor time so far.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the Junk Fee Prevention Act in the Senate on December 4, 2025, for himself and Senator Ruben Gallego.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
That referral is the last action on record: the bill sits in committee with no hearing, markup, vote, or cosponsors beyond its original two.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. To the extent anything has been decided, companies that profit from hidden fees — ticketing platforms, lodging operators, and telecom providers — are better off so far, because the bill has not moved toward becoming law.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the Junk Fee Prevention Act in the Senate.

for.name: Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, but no vote has occurred and no opposition is on record, so the partisan shape is not yet known.

industries.note: Primary and secondary ticket sellers would have to show all-in prices, disclose total ticket inventories 72 hours before sales, refund full amounts including fees, and flag speculative sales where they don't hold the ticket. These practices exist largely because drip pricing lets companies quote a low headline price and collect the difference in mandatory fees at checkout.

Lodging providers and booking platforms for stays under six months must include mandatory fees like resort and cleaning charges in the advertised total price. Resort fees in particular are charged to guests who cannot avoid them and rarely see them until booking.

Phone, internet, and cable companies could no longer charge early termination fees, must show a single aggregate price on bills, and must disclose when promotional rates expire and what the new rate will be. Providers currently use unitemized surcharges and surprise end-of-promo price jumps that raise what customers actually pay over the advertised rate.

Airlines would face quarterly reporting on ancillary fee revenue — bags, seat selection, changes and cancellations — published in a public carrier-by-carrier comparison. The bill requires transparency but does not cap or ban any of these fees, and ancillary fees have become a major revenue stream for carriers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has two sponsors and no committee action since referral, which is where comparable consumer-fee bills have typically stalled. Barring a hearing in the Senate Commerce Committee or attachment to a larger moving package, it will likely sit without a vote. Independently of Congress, the FTC and FCC could pursue some of the same fee-disclosure rules on their own authority.
